correctness.rationale: The left Hilbert A-module convention and exact complete Parseval and diagonal-multiplicity definitions were checked in the primary source. The proof reconstructs all quantifiers: a singleton Parseval vector in A is exactly an isometry, a k-fold diagonal Parseval vector is exactly k orthogonal isometries, and completeness follows by explicit module reconstruction. Two such isometries generate countably many via v^(j-1)w; absence of a pair forces k=1. The B(l2) shifts explicitly satisfy all original theorem hypotheses, and their nonzero orthogonal support projections meet rather than contradict the source final positive-sum bound.

originality.rationale: The primary 2023 article defines a left Hilbert module over any unital C*-algebra, and its Theorem 5.3 asserts a finite supremum for every group-like system with a wandering vector. Direct coefficient calculations establish that for the trivial system on A the finite admissible multiplicities are exactly the numbers of pairwise orthogonal isometries. The existence of two such isometries is precisely proper infiniteness of the unit, and yields infinitely many, while lack of a pair forces multiplicity one. The explicit B(l2) shifts make all hypotheses hold and the published positive-sum estimate remain bounded. Within-source Theorem 5.2 is the closest finite-level antecedent; it does not state or reconcile this dichotomy with Theorem 5.3.
residual_risks: An unindexed correction, thesis remark, or operator-algebra exposition could note the same inconsistency; absence from indexed search does not establish global novelty.

The existence of orthogonal isometries in properly infinite algebras is standard and the source itself gives a finite-level isometry criterion, so the novel scope is the exact invariant classification and explicit challenge to the universal finiteness assertion.
No analogue for general group-like unitary systems beyond the stated trivial-system case is claimed.

value.rationale: The corrected result attacks a headline universal finiteness theorem, not an incidental norm estimate. It gives an exact classification of the paper-defined multiplicity for a natural canonical class of systems: multiplicity is 1 or infinite, determined by proper infiniteness of the coefficient algebra. The explicit properly infinite example falsifies a central structural theorem despite a complete wandering vector, pinpointing the operator-order fallacy and clarifying the boundary between Hilbert-space finite scalar size and Hilbert C*-module projections.
